passage:
'Metro station within a ten-minute walk,' said Zeenat, writing on the back of an envelope. 'Otherwise one of us commutes two hours.'
'Must-have,' said Rajni. 'And a school nearby. We'll need one eventually.'
'Must-have. What about the balcony?'
'I love a balcony.'
'So do I. Would we skip a flat without one?'
Rajni thought about it. 'No. Nice-to-have.'
'Then it goes in the second column.' Zeenat drew a line down the paper. 'On Saturday, if a flat fails the first column, we don't even go inside.'
'And if it has a balcony but no school?'
'We thank the agent and leave.'
They both laughed. The argument over the last flat had lasted an hour. This one took about ten seconds.

qa.q: Where did the balcony go on Zeenat's list?
qa.a: The balcony went in the second column as a nice-to-have.

qa.q: What does the laugh after "We thank the agent and leave" suggest Rajni and Zeenat are feeling?
qa.a: It suggests they feel relaxed and united, glad that the list has made the choice simple.

qa.q: What could they do if no flat meets everything in the first column?
qa.a: They could talk over which must-haves are truly essential or widen the search area, instead of dropping the list, because it still keeps their talks short.

qa.q: How might the agent find their approach?
qa.a: The agent may find it helpful, since a clear list means fewer wasted trips and only fitting flats to show.

grounding: Rajni and Zeenat separate must-haves from an optional balcony to keep viewings focused and arguments short.

passage:
Before the first viewing, Ujjwal and I sat on the steps of our rented building in Hyderabad with one sheet of paper and two columns.
Must-haves: under fifteen minutes' walk to a metro station, because we both commute. A decent school nearby, because we're planning a baby in the next couple of years. Two bedrooms. Within budget.
Nice-to-haves: a balcony, a gym in the complex, an east-facing kitchen, which my mother cares about more than I do.
The first flat we saw had a gorgeous balcony. I fell a little in love. Then Ujjwal quietly asked the agent how far the metro was. Twenty-five minutes by auto. We looked at the sheet and left.
The fifth one had no balcony at all, but was six minutes from the metro and next to a school. We didn't even argue.
— Rukmini

qa.q: How far was the metro from the first flat?
How did Rukmini feel about the first flat's balcony, and what helped?
qa.a: Rukmini fell a little in love with the balcony, but the must-have list helped Rukmini let it go without disappointment turning into an argument.

qa.q: What else could Rukmini and Ujjwal add to their list?
qa.a: They could add a budget line with the maximum price, and check it at every viewing along with the must-haves.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal see the list during the viewings?
qa.a: Ujjwal can point to the metro rule calmly instead of arguing, so the list lets Ujjwal raise concerns without seeming negative.

grounding: It shows a couple agreeing must-haves such as metro access and a nearby school and treating a balcony as optional, keeping viewings focused and disagreements short.

passage:
Property agent's note — client file, Deepika and Harish, Whitefield. Written by Nazia.

I've shown flats to many couples. These two made my job much easier.
At our first meeting Deepika handed me a printed list. Must-haves: walking distance to the new metro line, a school within two kilometres, two bedrooms, lift. Nice-to-haves: balcony, covered parking, a park nearby.
At the third viewing, Harish loved a flat with a huge balcony facing the lake. Deepika checked the list and asked me about the school. Four kilometres. They looked at each other, and Harish said, "Balcony's on the other column." We moved on in two minutes.
The seventh flat had no balcony but met every must-have. They made an offer that week.
What I did next: I've started asking all my clients to bring the same kind of list.

qa.q: How far was the school from the third flat?
What might Harish have been feeling on saying "Balcony's on the other column"?
qa.a: Harish was probably disappointed to let the lake-view balcony go but also calm and accepting, trusting the list they had agreed.

qa.q: What else could Deepika and Harish do before making the offer?
qa.a: They could get the documents checked by a lawyer and confirm their loan eligibility with the bank.

qa.q: How does the couple's list look to the agent?
qa.a: The agent finds it makes viewings quicker and clearer, so much so that the agent now asks other clients to bring a similar list.

grounding: It shows, through an agent's note, a couple using agreed must-haves like metro access and a nearby school and treating a balcony as optional to keep viewings focused.
